cards.title: Köhler · circle representation and equal diagonals
cards.aim: Can reorganizing how a problem is represented make a hidden relationship usable?
cards.manipulated: Not a comparison of groups; it is a demonstration of how representing the circle problem as a rectangle changes the solution.
cards.measured: Finding the length of line x when the circle's radius is r.
cards.found: Seeing the black line as a diagonal of a rectangle makes it equal to the dashed radius (the other diagonal), so x = r.
cards.means: Restructuring the representation, not new calculation, makes the answer available.
cards.trap: Do not treat x as an isolated unknown inside the circle; the key is spotting the rectangle with equal diagonals.

cards.title: Metcalfe and Wiebe · insight puzzles and warmth judgments
cards.aim: Do people feel gradually closer to a solution for insight problems as they do for noninsight problems?
cards.manipulated: Problem type: insight problems (triangle and chain) vs noninsight problems (algebra).
cards.measured: Warmth ratings (hot means close to the solution) given every 15 seconds while solving.
cards.found: For algebra, warmth rose gradually as the solution approached. For insight problems, warmth stayed low until close to the solution and then jumped sharply, from about 3 to 7.
cards.means: Insight solutions come with a sudden change in felt progress, unlike methodical noninsight solving.
cards.trap: Not all problem solving is sudden; the sudden jump describes insight problems, not algebra.

cards.title: Candle problem · matchbox presentation and functional fixedness
cards.aim: Does seeing an object only in its familiar use block its use for something else?
cards.manipulated: Whether the matches were inside the box or the matchboxes were empty.
cards.measured: Whether participants solved the problem of mounting the candle on a vertical corkboard so it burns without dripping wax on the floor.
cards.found: Participants given empty matchboxes were twice as likely to solve the problem.
cards.means: Functional fixedness: treating the box only as a container hides its use as a platform for the candle.
cards.trap: The materials were enough to solve it; the obstacle was the familiar use of the box.

cards.title: Two-string problem · pliers as a weight and a movement hint
cards.aim: What helps people see a new use for an object in the two-string problem?
cards.manipulated: Whether an experimenter 'accidentally' set a string in motion (the hint).
cards.measured: Whether participants solved the problem of tying together two strings hanging too far apart to reach.
cards.found: After the swinging hint, most participants were able to solve the problem. The solution is to tie the pliers on a string as a weight and make it swing like a pendulum.
cards.means: The hint helped restructure the representation, so the string became something that can be swung within reach.
cards.trap: The pliers' useful property is their weight, not their ability to grip; that is the functional fixedness.

cards.title: Water-jug problems · practice and a simpler available solution
cards.aim: Can a method that worked earlier block a simpler solution?
cards.manipulated: Practice with the early problems that Practice with early problems solved by B − A − 2C, then new problems (7 and 8) with capacities where a simpler solution exists.
cards.measured: Not measured with participants on the slide; it traces which solution method each problem allows.
cards.found: Repeated success with B − A − 2C builds a mental set. In problem 7 the goal 18 can be reached by A + C, and in problem 8 the goal 25 by A − C, but the familiar method still works and is brought first.
cards.means: A mental set can inhibit a simpler solution even when the familiar one remains possible.
cards.trap: The familiar method still works in problems 7 and 8; the set blocks the simpler one, not the correct answer.

cards.title: Search demonstrations · tile puzzle and Tower of Hanoi subgoals
cards.aim: How can solving be described as search through a problem space using operators and subgoals?
cards.manipulated: Nothing varied; these are worked demonstrations with the Tower of Hanoi and a numbered-tile puzzle.
cards.measured: Not measured with participants; the slides trace states, legal moves, and subgoals.
cards.found: Operators set which moves are legal; routes pass through intermediate states; a search tree shows branches of alternative states. In the Tower of Hanoi, subgoals free the large disk, free the third peg, then move the large disk.
cards.means: Means–end analysis reduces the difference between the current state and the goal by achieving subgoals.
cards.trap: A subgoal is an intermediate condition that makes a move possible, not the final answer.

cards.title: Mutilated checkerboard · labels, pairing, and think-aloud protocols
cards.aim: Does how a problem is stated change how hard it is to find the pairing constraint?
cards.manipulated: Information on the board: blank, colored, labeled black and pink, or labeled bread and butter.
cards.measured: How fast participants solved the covering problem, along with think-aloud reports of their thoughts.
cards.found: Participants solved the bread-and-butter condition twice as fast as the blank condition. Think-aloud reports showed a shift from squares as positions to the relation between the two kinds of square.
cards.means: Labels pointing to the right representation (one of each kind per domino) reduce solving time, matching Gestalt restructuring.
cards.trap: Equal total area (62 squares, 31 dominoes) does not mean a covering is possible; the colors are unequal.

cards.title: Marriage and checkerboard · mapping a shared pairing constraint
cards.aim: Can a solver see why 31 pairs are impossible when the two groups are unequal?
cards.manipulated: The number of men and women (32 and 32, then 30 and 32), and the matching board problem with two same-colored corners removed.
cards.measured: Whether 31 heterosexual marriages (or 31 dominoes) can be formed.
cards.found: No. With 30 men and 32 women, at most 30 marriages are possible. The checkerboard has the same imbalance between square colors, so 31 dominoes cannot cover it.
cards.means: The solution comes from the one-of-each pairing relationship, not from total size or area.
cards.trap: Total count (62 people or 62 squares) says 31 pairs, but the pairing rule is what decides it.

cards.title: Duncker and Gick–Holyoak · radiation, fortress, and reminders
cards.aim: Do people notice and use a solved source story (the fortress) to solve the radiation problem?
cards.manipulated: Whether participants read the fortress story first, and whether they were told to think about that story.
cards.measured: Whether participants reached the converging-rays solution to the radiation problem.
cards.found: About 10% solved radiation without the analogy. After reading the fortress story, about 30% solved it. When told to think about the story, about 75% did.
cards.means: Having a useful source in memory is not enough. People must notice it and map it to the target.
cards.trap: Many people read the source but do not spontaneously use it. The hint is the difference between 30% and 75%.

cards.title: Lightbulb transfer · surface and structural similarities
cards.aim: Does a source with similar surface features, or similar structure, help solve a target problem?
cards.manipulated: Which source participants knew: radiation, fragile-glass lightbulb, or insufficient-intensity lightbulb. A control group had no source.
cards.measured: Whether participants solved the target (lightbulb or radiation).
cards.found: 81% who knew radiation solved the lightbulb problem, versus 10% in the control group. 69% who read the fragile-glass solution solved radiation, versus 33% after the insufficient-intensity version.
cards.means: Matching structure (a strong effect at the target plus protected surroundings) helps more than matching only the objects.
cards.trap: Both lightbulb sources use converging lasers, but only the fragile-glass one shares the reason (damage to surroundings).

cards.title: In vivo observation · analogies in scientific work
cards.aim: How often do real scientists use analogies during ordinary work?
cards.manipulated: Nothing was manipulated. Researchers observed scientists in real-world lab meetings.
cards.measured: The number of analogies used in a one-hour laboratory meeting.
cards.found: Scientists use about 3-15 analogies in a one-hour laboratory meeting.
cards.means: Analogies are common in real work even though they are hard to transfer in lab tasks (the analogical paradox).
cards.trap: In vivo gives real context but little control of variables, and it can be time-consuming.

cards.title: Chase and Simon · game positions, random layouts, and chunks
cards.aim: Is expert chess recall due to general memory or to organized knowledge?
cards.manipulated: Skill (chess master versus a beginner with under 100 hours) and the arrangement type (actual game positions versus random arrangements).
cards.measured: Reproducing the piece positions after viewing the board for five seconds.
cards.found: The expert did much better than the beginner on actual game positions. The same familiar chunks were not available for random arrangements.
cards.means: Expert memory depends on chunks stored in long-term memory, not on a general memory advantage.
cards.trap: Do not say experts remember everything better. The advantage is tied to meaningful positions.

cards.title: Chi and colleagues · surface-based and principle-based sorting
cards.aim: Do experts and novices organize physics problems in the same way?
cards.manipulated: Group: experts (physics professors) versus novices (students with one semester of physics).
cards.measured: Sorting 24 physics problems into groups by similarity.
cards.found: Novices grouped by surface features, such as inclined planes. Experts grouped by structural features, such as conservation of energy.
cards.means: Expertise changes which relationship is used as the basis for similarity.
cards.trap: The same problem 24 pairs with 23 (novice, inclined planes) or with 21 (expert, conservation of energy).

existing_explainers.title: Tower of Hanoi with subgoals
existing_explainers.plain: You cannot move the big disk until it is free and the target peg is free, so you set up those conditions first.
steps: Goal: move the large disk to the third peg.
Subgoal 1: free the large disk by moving the smallest disk to the third peg and the next disk to the middle peg.
Subgoal 2: free the third peg by moving the smallest disk from the third peg onto the smaller stack on the middle peg.
Subgoal 3: move the largest disk from the starting peg to the third peg.
Then move the smaller disks onto it, never putting a larger disk on a smaller one.
existing_explainers.example: The slide's example: the smallest disk goes to the third peg, the next disk to the middle peg, then the smallest goes onto the middle stack.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Achieving a subgoal is not the finished puzzle; the smaller disks still have to reach the third peg.
explain: Newell and Simon (1956) treated problem solving as a search that happens between the posing of a problem and its solution, where the Gestalt tradition had looked only at the starting structure and the structure reached once it is solved. Every problem has an initial state, intermediate states along the way, and a goal state, and operators are the rules that say which moves are allowed and carry you from one state to another. In the Tower of Hanoi, the stack of three disks starts on the first peg and must end in the same order on the third. Disks move one at a time, only when nothing is on top, and never onto a smaller disk.

The goal is easy to picture, which is what makes people go wrong. The stack cannot move all at once, so heading straight for the goal fails. Smaller disks keep having to get out of the way, and the middle peg serves as a temporary parking spot. The number of moves explodes as disks are added: with 64 disks it would take a trillion years, even at one correct move per second.

Means-end analysis is the strategy that tames this. It aims to reduce the differences between the initial state and the goal state, and it relies on subgoals, which are smaller goals that create intermediate states closer to the goal. The main difference is that the whole stack is on the wrong peg, and the largest disk cannot move until the disks above it are cleared. The first subgoal is therefore to free the large disk: the smallest disk goes from the first peg to the third, and the middle disk goes from the first peg to the middle peg.

The second subgoal is to free the third peg. The smallest disk moves from the third peg onto the middle disk, so the two smaller disks sit legally together on the middle peg and the large disk has a place to go. The third subgoal is to move the large disk onto the third peg, where it is in its final place. Putting the smallest disk on the third peg and then taking it off looks wasteful, but that detour frees the space the large disk needs, and means-end analysis accepts detours that remove an obstacle.

Reaching the third subgoal is not finishing, because the same strategy still has to move the two smaller disks onto the large one. A heavy piano shows the pattern. It sits in the living room under a pile of chairs, and the bedroom it is headed for is full of boxes, so the question stops being how to move the piano and becomes what is stopping it. The chairs go to the hallway, the boxes follow, and only then does the piano roll in. Setting the chairs aside looks pointless on its own, but each act removes a specific obstacle, just like parking a small disk. When the piano is in place, the chairs and boxes still have to be arranged around it, as the smaller disks still have to be stacked on the large one.

existing_explainers.title: Mutilated checkerboard
existing_explainers.plain: Each domino covers one square of each color, so the board must have equal numbers of the two colors.
steps: A full board has 64 squares and takes 32 dominoes.
Remove two opposite corners and 62 squares remain, matching 31 dominoes in area.
Every domino covers one square of each color.
Opposite corners are the same color, so one color now has fewer squares.
Equal numbers are needed, so no covering is possible.
existing_explainers.example: The bread-and-butter labels make it clear that each domino needs one bread and one butter.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Equal area (62 squares, 31 dominoes) does not guarantee a legal covering.
explain: A checkerboard has 64 squares and can be completely covered by 32 dominoes, each covering 2 neighboring squares. The mutilated checkerboard problem removes two opposite corners and asks whether the remaining 62 squares can be covered with 31 dominoes. It is hard because the numbers seem to fit: 31 dominoes at two squares each cover exactly 62 squares. The arithmetic suggests a covering exists, so people start laying dominoes down one at a time, which could take a very long time and could never prove that a covering is impossible.

The answer is no, and the colors of the squares hold the key. Neighboring squares are always different colors, so every domino covers one dark square and one light square. Opposite corners share the same color, so removing them leaves 32 squares of one color and 30 of the other. Thirty-one dominoes would need 31 squares of each color, so a full covering is impossible. Once the board is represented by its colors, a single count settles the question before any domino is placed. Equal area, 62 squares and 31 dominoes, is never enough; the covering also needs equal numbers of the two colors.

The key is understanding two things: each domino covers two squares, and those squares must be of different colors. Experimental conditions differed in how much information was given about the squares. Condition 1 was a blank board, condition 2 a colored board, condition 3 wrote the words black and pink on the squares, and condition 4 wrote the words bread and butter. The bread and butter condition emphasized the difference between the squares, since bread and butter naturally come in pairs, one of each, and participants solved it twice as fast as the blank condition. The board and dominoes were identical throughout, so only the representation changed.

A school dance shows the same logic. With 62 students in the gym and a rule that every dancer needs a partner, one leader and one follower, 62 people can form 31 pairs. Matching students up one pair after pair could take all evening. A glance at the name tags showing 32 leaders and only 30 followers settles it at once, because 31 pairs would need 31 of each kind. The problem was never about total head count but about the two kinds. The removed corners are like sending two followers home.

Think-aloud protocols show this shift happening. Before participants realize that the words bread and butter are important, they talk about laying down dominoes, and afterward they talk about pairing the two kinds of squares. That is similar to the Gestalt idea of a representational shift. The way the squares are described is what lets the solver see that the numbers matching up does not matter, and that the kinds matching up does.

existing_explainers.title: Chain problem
existing_explainers.plain: Treat a whole section of chain as the source of connectors instead of opening one link at a time.
steps: Opening a link costs 2 cents and closing it costs 3 cents, so opening and closing one link costs 5 cents.
The budget is 15 cents, so you can open and close three links.
Open the three links of one three-link section.
Use each opened link to join the other three sections into a closed loop, closing each once.
existing_explainers.example: Four short sections become one closed loop for exactly 15 cents.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Opening and closing one link costs 5 cents, so 15 cents allows only three links; use one whole section as the connectors.
explain: The chain problem was one of the insight problems used by Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987), who designed an experiment to distinguish insight from noninsight problems. The triangle problem and the chain problem were the insight problems, and algebra problems were the noninsight ones. Participants gave warmth judgments every 15 seconds, rating how close they felt to the answer. Metcalfe and Wiebe expected that in insight problems people would not be good at predicting how near they were to a solution, because if insight comes suddenly the solver should feel far away right until the answer arrives.

The task is to join four short pieces of chain, each with three links, into a single closed loop. Opening a link costs 2 cents, closing a link costs 3 cents, and only 15 cents is available. The obvious plan opens one link on each piece and uses it to join the next piece. That is four links at 2 to open and 3 to close, which is 20 cents and goes over budget. Opening and closing one link costs 5 cents, so 15 cents allows only three links, and the obvious plan needs four.

The answer comes from seeing the parts differently. Open all three links of one piece and use those three open links to join the other three pieces into a loop, closing each once. That costs 3 times (2 plus 3), which is exactly 15 cents. The shift is treating one whole piece of chain as a set of connectors instead of as a piece to be joined.

Making a bracelet from four short pieces, each made of three metal rings, works the same way when a jeweler will open and close only three rings in total. Opening one ring on every piece to join it to the next needs four and fails when counted. One piece has to be sacrificed as a supply of parts: its three rings are opened once each and used as connectors for the other three pieces. The sacrificed piece stops being a piece and becomes a bag of connectors, and the count comes to exactly three.

This answer does not come from gradual improvement, and trying the first plan harder never helps. It requires leaving the obvious approach behind, and because the problem looks simple, the obvious approach is hard to give up. This is the kind of restructuring that Gestalt psychologists linked to insight. Steadily rising warmth would mean gradual progress, while low warmth followed by a sudden jump means insight, and that is the pattern found with these problems.

existing_explainers.title: Triangle problem
existing_explainers.plain: Move three dots from a ten-dot upward triangle so it points down, keeping seven in place.
steps: Start with ten dots in four rows, with the point on top.
Move the original top dot to a new bottom point beneath the center of the original bottom row.
Move the two outer dots of the original bottom row to the outer ends of the original two-dot row.
That row now has four dots, with three, two, and one below it.
existing_explainers.example: Only three dots move and seven stay put, giving a downward-pointing triangle.
explain: The triangle problem is the second of the insight problems used by Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987). They compared insight problems, the triangle and chain problems, with noninsight algebra problems, and asked participants for warmth judgments every 15 seconds, rating from cold to hot how close they felt to the answer. With noninsight problems, which involve a more methodical process, people know how close they are because every finished step brings the answer visibly closer. With insight problems, people should not be very good at predicting how near they are, because the solution arrives suddenly.

The task is to move three of the blue dots so the triangle points to the bottom of the page. The triangle has ten dots arranged in rows of one, two, three and four, with the point on top, and the rule is that seven dots stay where they are while only three move. It is hard because the problem looks simple, which makes the obvious approach hard to give up, and the obvious approach does not work.

The top dot, the one at the point, goes below the middle of the bottom row. The two ends of the bottom row go up beside the row of two dots. The row that held two dots now has four, and below it sit the rows of three, two and one. The rows run four, three, two and one, so the triangle points down, and only three dots moved.

A team photo with players in rows of one, two, three and four, narrow at the front and wide at the back, shows why nudging fails. If the coach asks for the formation to point the other way with only three players moving, the natural instinct is to shift everybody a little in hope that it slowly turns into the new shape. It never gets there, because small nudges keep the old shape intact. What works is to see the team as people who can be regrouped, leave most of them in place, and move only the player at the old point and the two at the ends of the back row, placing them at the opposite end.

Nothing about this comes from gradual improvement. You cannot get nearer by small adjustments; you have to give up the picture of an upward triangle and see the dots as parts that can be regrouped. That is the restructuring that Gestalt psychologists linked to insight. It explains why warmth stays low and then jumps, from feeling cold to knowing you have it, instead of rising steadily.

existing_explainers.title: Water-jug problems and mental set
existing_explainers.plain: A rule that worked on early problems can stop you seeing a shorter route later.
steps: Early problems use B − A − 2C, for example 127 − 21 − 3 − 3 = 100.
Problem 7 (A 15, B 39, C 3, goal 18): the familiar way is 39 − 15 − 6 = 18, but A + C gives 18 directly.
Problem 8 (A 28, B 59, C 3, goal 25): A − C gives 25 directly, although B − A − 2C also works.
existing_explainers.example: Problem 8: 28 − 3 = 25 is simpler than the familiar method.
existing_explainers.watchOut: The familiar method still works in problems 7 and 8; the issue is that it blocks the simpler one.
explain: A mental set is a preconceived notion about how to approach a problem, based on a person's past experiences with the problem or with similar problems. It is a broader form of fixation: a method that worked before gets used again, even when a better method is available. The water-jug problem reveals how it works. The task is to obtain a required volume of water, given three empty jars for measuring. Each problem gives the capacities of jugs A, B and C and a final desired quantity, in quarts, and only filling, pouring and emptying are allowed.

In problem 1 the jugs hold 21, 127 and 3 quarts and the target is 100. Fill jug B with 127 quarts and pour from B into A until A is full, which leaves 106 quarts in B. Pour from B into C until C is full, empty C and fill it once more, which leaves exactly 100 quarts in B. The formula is B minus A minus twice C, or 127 minus 21 minus 2 times 3, which is 100. The same formula solves each of the early problems.

That success has a cost. Participants started applying the formula automatically, and that automatic habit is the mental set. It forms because the formula keeps working. Later problems test the habit. Problem 7 has jugs of 15, 39 and 3 quarts and a target of 18. The long formula still works, giving 39 minus 15 minus 6, but simply adding A and C, 15 plus 3, gives 18 directly. Problem 8 has jugs of 28, 59 and 3 and a target of 25, which A minus C solves directly, 28 minus 3, even though the familiar formula also works.

Walking to class along the main road for weeks works the same way. It has never failed, so you stop thinking about it, and when a footpath opens through the park that would halve the trip, you are on autopilot and walk past the entrance. The main road did not stop working. Because it worked so many times, you stopped looking for anything else, and the shorter way sat in plain view. Someone new to campus, with no habit, would probably spot the footpath at once.

The experiment shows that the mental set inhibited participants from using the simpler solutions, and people who had not worked through the earlier problems found the short methods far more often. A set speeds up solving when problems are alike, but once the problems change, the same set hides the easier paths. Past success can therefore become an obstacle in its own right. The familiar method is not wrong in problems 7 and 8; it blocks the simpler one.

existing_explainers.title: Pairing problems: marriage and checkerboard
existing_explainers.plain: Count the two kinds of pieces that must pair up. If the counts differ, a full pairing is impossible.
steps: Find what each pair must contain (one man and one woman, or one square of each color).
Count each kind.
Compare the counts, not the total.
If unequal, some are left over, however you rearrange.
existing_explainers.example: 30 men and 32 women give at most 30 marriages. Removing two same-colored corners leaves unequal colors, so 31 dominoes cannot cover the board.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Do not use total size (62 divided by 2 = 31).
explain: A pairing problem is decided by what each pair must contain, not by how many pieces there are in total. A checkerboard has 64 squares, and 32 dominoes, each covering two neighboring squares, cover it completely. Cut off two opposite corners and 62 squares remain. Thirty-one dominoes cover 62 squares, so the numbers seem to fit and people start laying dominoes down, but no number of failed attempts would ever prove a covering impossible.

The colors decide it. Neighboring squares are always different colors, so every domino, wherever it lands, covers exactly one dark square and one light square. Opposite corners are the same color, so removing them takes away two squares of one color. What remains is 32 squares of one color and 30 of the other, and 31 dominoes would need 31 squares of each color. That balance is simply not there, so the board cannot be covered, and counting the colors settles the question before any domino is placed.

The Russian marriage problem has the same structure in a form where it is easy to see. A village has 32 bachelors and 32 unmarried women, and the matchmaker has arranged 32 marriages. Then two bachelors die, and the question is whether she can arrange 31 marriages among the 62 survivors. Every marriage pairs one man with one woman, and there are now 30 men and 32 women, so at most 30 marriages are possible and two women are left over. Sixty-two people would make 31 pairs only if anyone could pair with anyone, but each pair needs one person from each group, so the smaller group sets the limit.

This is analogical transfer, with the marriage story as the source problem and the checkerboard as the target. The parts map one to one: men and women are the two colors of squares, marriages are dominoes, and the two dead bachelors are the two missing corners. Each leftover square corresponds to a woman without a partner. Because the mapping is complete, the reasoning from the source carries straight over, and rearranging the dominoes more cleverly cannot help, since the imbalance between the two kinds rules out the last pair.

A shoe store that sells shoes only as matched pairs shows the same logic. Someone wheels in a cart with 30 left shoes and 32 right shoes and asks how many pairs can be sold. The answer is not 31 just because there are 62 shoes in all. A pair needs one of each kind, so the lefts and the rights are counted separately and the smaller pile decides: 30 pairs, with two right shoes left on the cart however they are shuffled. The shoes are the squares or the people, and a pair is a domino or a marriage. Whenever the counts of the two kinds are unequal, some pieces are left over, so the whole method is to ask what each pair must contain and count those things.

existing_explainers.title: Converging solution (radiation, fortress, lightbulb)
existing_explainers.plain: Split a strong effect into weak parts that travel separately and meet at the target.
steps: Find the target that needs a strong effect.
Find the limit on the paths (healthy tissue, mines, fragile glass).
Use several weak approaches from different directions.
Make them arrive together.
existing_explainers.example: Several low-intensity rays hit the tumor at once. Each path is safe, and the combined intensity destroys it.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Dividing without combining at the same time does not work.
explain: Duncker's radiation problem sets two demands against each other. A patient has an inoperable malignant tumor in his stomach, and a kind of ray can destroy the tumor if it arrives all at once at a high enough intensity. At that intensity the healthy tissue the rays pass through on the way is destroyed too. At lower intensities the rays are harmless to the tissue, but they do nothing to the tumor either. The tumor needs high intensity and the tissue needs low intensity, so no single ray can satisfy both, and only 10% of participants reach the answer without help.

The answer is to send several low-intensity rays from different directions so that they converge on the tumor at the same time. Each ray is weak enough to pass through healthy tissue safely, and where they meet, their combined strength destroys the tumor. The strong effect exists only at the point where the weak parts meet.

A chef who wants to brown the sugar on one spot of a dessert faces the same shape. The dish and table underneath are delicate and would scorch under a hot flame. One strong burner would brown the spot and ruin everything it passes over, and one gentle lamp keeps everything safe but browns nothing. Several gentle lamps aimed at the same spot from different sides solve it, because anywhere along the way only one lamp shines and the surroundings feel something mild, while at the point where all the beams cross the warmth adds up enough to brown the sugar. When something needs a strong effect in one place and a weak effect everywhere else, the strength is split into weak pieces that travel separate paths and arrive together.

The fortress problem has this same structure. A rebel general knows his whole army could take a dictator's fortress, but the roads are mined so that only small groups pass safely, and a large force would blow up the road and the neighboring villages. He divides the army into small groups, sends them along different roads, and has them arrive at the same time. The fortress is the tumor, the small groups are the low-intensity rays, the roads are the paths through tissue, and the mines are the healthy tissue.

Noticing a good analogy is hard. After reading the fortress story, only 30% solved the radiation problem, against 10% without it, and 70% did not see the correspondences by themselves. Gick and Holyoak described three steps: noticing the analogy, which is the most difficult, mapping the parts of the source onto the target, and applying the mapping to produce a parallel solution. Failing at any one blocks the answer. When participants were told to think about the story they had read, success rose to 75%, so noticing is the main barrier.

Similarity of surface features makes noticing much easier. In the lightbulb problem, a strong laser aimed at a broken filament would break the fragile glass around it, while a weak laser would not fuse the filament. Rays and lasers, tumors and filaments, and tissue and glass are close enough that the link comes to mind easily. Eighty-one percent of participants who knew the radiation problem solved the lightbulb problem, against 10% of the control group, which had no source. The radiation problem worked far better as a source than the fortress story, which helped only 30%, because it shares both the structure and the surface features of the target.

qa_facts.q: What makes something a problem, and why does knowing the goal not mean the problem is solved?
qa_facts.a: A problem has a present state, a goal and an obstacle between them, and the solution is not immediately obvious. The present state is the situation as it is, the goal is the situation you are trying to reach, and the obstacle blocks an immediate move from one to the other. In the numbered-tile puzzle you can state exactly what the finished arrangement looks like and still have a problem, because the sequence of moves that gets there is unclear. The difficulty is the route, not whether the goal has been stated.

qa_facts.q: What is the Gestalt approach to problem solving (Koffka, 1935), and what is restructuring in Köhler’s circle problem?
qa_facts.a: The Gestalt approach takes a perceptual view of problem solving, associated with Koffka (1935). A problem is represented in the mind, so how a person organizes it affects which solution becomes available. Restructuring means reorganizing the representation so a hidden relationship becomes usable. In Köhler’s circle problem you must find the length of line x when the radius is r. The black line is one diagonal of a rectangle whose lower-right corner is at the circle’s center, and the dashed line from the upper-left corner on the circle to the center is a radius. The two diagonals of a rectangle are equal, so x = r.

qa_facts.q: What is insight, and does every problem get solved with an Aha experience?
qa_facts.a: Insight is the sudden realization of a problem’s solution. A person first perceives an object or problem one way and then represents it differently, and discovering a crucial element in the changed representation makes the solution available all at once. Gestalt psychologists connected this with the Aha experience, a sudden change from not having the solution to recognizing it. Not every problem is solved this way, because some allow a more methodical process in which successive operations bring the person closer to an answer.

qa_facts.q: What did Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) do and find with insight and algebra problems?
qa_facts.a: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) compared insight problems, the triangle and chain problems, with noninsight problems such as algebra. Every 15 seconds participants gave warmth ratings of how close they felt to a solution, with hot meaning close and colder meaning far. The prediction was that for insight problems people would not be good at anticipating how near they were, because a change in representation can make the answer appear without growing feelings of progress. For algebra, warmth ratings rose gradually as the solution approached. For insight problems, warmth stayed low until close to the solution and then jumped sharply, from about 3 to 7.

qa_facts.q: How are the triangle problem and the chain problem solved in Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987)?
qa_facts.a: In Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987), the triangle problem has ten dots that form an upward-pointing triangle and you must move exactly three dots to make it point down, with seven staying in place. The original top dot becomes a new bottom point beneath the center of the original bottom row, and the two outer dots of the original bottom row move to the ends of the two-dot row, giving rows of four, three, two and one. In the chain problem, four short sections of chain must become one closed loop. Opening a link costs 2 cents, closing it costs 3 cents, and the budget is 15 cents, so three open-and-close operations are possible. One three-link section is opened into three separate links, and those links connect the other three sections into a closed loop, using the full 15 cents.

qa_facts.q: What are fixation and functional fixedness, and what happens in the candle problem?
qa_facts.a: Fixation is a tendency to focus on one characteristic of a problem in a way that blocks a solution, and Gestalt psychologists saw it as a major obstacle. Functional fixedness restricts an object to its familiar function. In the candle problem you have a candle, matches and their box, and tacks, and must mount the candle on a corkboard so wax does not drip on the floor. The solution is to tack the matchbox to the board and use it as a platform. Seeing the box only as a container for matches blocks that, and participants given empty matchboxes were twice as likely to solve it.

qa_facts.q: How do the two-string problem and the swinging-string hint show functional fixedness and restructuring?
qa_facts.a: In the two-string problem you must tie together two strings hanging too far apart to reach both at once. A pair of pliers can be tied to one string as a weight so it swings like a pendulum, and you catch it while holding the other string. The familiar grip function of the pliers blocks seeing the weight. When an experimenter accidentally set a string in motion, most participants solved the problem, because the hint restructured the representation, so the string became something that could be made to swing within reach.

qa_facts.q: What is a mental set, and how do the water-jug problems show it?
qa_facts.a: A mental set is a preconceived notion about how to approach a problem, based on past experience with that problem or similar ones. It concerns the method of solving, so a person keeps applying a familiar procedure even when another approach would work. In the water-jug problems you get three empty jugs with given capacities and a target amount. In the first problem A holds 21, B holds 127, C holds 3 and the goal is 100, and the solution is B − A − 2C. Repeated success with that procedure makes it the expected method. In problem 7 (A 15, B 39, C 3, goal 18) the familiar method still works, but A + C gives 18 more directly. In problem 8 (A 28, B 59, C 3, goal 25) A − C gives 25 directly. The mental set inhibits the simpler solution even though the familiar one remains possible.

qa_facts.q: What did Newell and Simon (1956) mean by problem solving as search through a problem space?
qa_facts.a: Newell and Simon (1956) developed the Logic Theorist and described problem solving as a search that happens between posing a problem and reaching its solution. A problem space includes the initial state, the intermediate states along the way and the goal state. Knowing the initial and goal states does not tell you which intermediate states connect them, so solving means finding a sequence that reaches the goal.

qa_facts.q: What are operators, and how do they work in the Tower of Hanoi?
qa_facts.a: Operators are the rules that say which moves are allowed, and applying one changes the problem from one state to another. In the Tower of Hanoi you move one disk at a time, you can only move a disk with nothing on top of it, and a larger disk can never be placed on a smaller one, even in intermediate arrangements. The starting stack is the initial state, the completed stack on the target peg is the goal state, and temporary distributions across the pegs are intermediate states. Smaller disks have to be moved out of the way repeatedly, and the 64-disk version would take roughly a trillion years at one move per second.

qa_facts.q: What are the initial, intermediate and goal states in the numbered-tile puzzle, and what is a search tree?
qa_facts.a: The puzzle has eight tiles and one empty space on a three-by-three board. The initial state is 8–empty–6, 5–4–7, 2–3–1, and the goal state is empty–1–2, 3–4–5, 6–7–8. A tile being on the board does not mean it is in its required position, so the whole arrangement defines the state. A search tree shows the possible states and the moves connecting them. From a start such as 2–8–3, 1–6–4, 7–empty–5, the empty space can shift left, up or right by swapping with an adjacent tile, and each result is a different intermediate state with the same eight tiles. Each state can have several successors, so the solver chooses which branches to pursue, and a connected sequence of states supplies a route to the goal.

qa_facts.q: What is means–end analysis, and what are the subgoals in the Tower of Hanoi?
qa_facts.a: Newell and Simon’s approach to solving as search leads to means–end analysis, which organizes the search around reducing the difference between the current situation and the goal. A subgoal is a condition that makes part of the larger task possible, not the final answer. In the Tower of Hanoi the large disk cannot move while smaller disks sit on it, so the first subgoal is freeing the large disk. The smallest disk goes to the third peg and the next disk to the middle peg. The third peg must then be free for the large disk, so the second subgoal is freeing the third peg, by moving the smallest disk from the third peg onto the smaller stack on the middle peg. The third subgoal is moving the large disk from the starting peg to the third peg, and the smaller disks still have to be brought over afterward. Different subgoals address different obstacles to the same move, one at the source and one at the destination.

qa_facts.q: How does the mutilated-checkerboard problem work, and why is covering it impossible?
qa_facts.a: An ordinary checkerboard has 64 squares and 32 dominoes can cover it, with each domino covering two adjacent squares of different colors. In the mutilated version two opposite corners are removed, leaving 62 squares, which matches the area of 31 dominoes. But the two removed corners are the same color, so the board has fewer squares of that color, and every domino covers one square of each color. The covering would need equal numbers of the two colors, so it is impossible. Equal total area does not guarantee a legal arrangement, and the color imbalance applies to every possible placement.

qa_facts.q: What did the bread-and-butter condition show about how a problem is stated?
qa_facts.a: How a problem is stated changes its difficulty. Participants got a blank board, a colored board, a board labeled black and pink, or one labeled bread and butter. The bread-and-butter labels emphasized the difference between the square types and their pairing, which made it easier to represent a domino as needing one of each kind. Participants in that condition solved the problem twice as fast as those in the blank condition.

qa_facts.q: What is a think-aloud protocol, and what does it reveal in the bread-and-butter checkerboard problem?
qa_facts.a: A think-aloud protocol asks a person to say aloud what they are thinking while solving, verbalizing new thoughts and not just describing their actions. In the bread-and-butter version, participants can reach the solution once they recognize that the words bread and butter matter for the required pairing. Their thinking shifts from treating squares as positions to considering the relationship between the two kinds of square. That is a representational shift related to the Gestalt account of restructuring, since the objects and the covering requirement stay the same but the solver uses a different relationship among them. Verbal reports can show when the pairing enters the person’s reasoning.

qa_facts.q: How do representation and insight, search, and problem statement each affect problem solving?
qa_facts.a: Reorganization and insight concern how a problem is represented, since a person may organize the elements so that a useful relationship is hidden, and reorganizing can make the solution available, sometimes suddenly. Problem solving as search concerns the activity between posing a problem and reaching its solution, finding a route through possible states, and naming the start and goal does not give the route. How a problem is stated affects difficulty because the presentation influences which relationships a person represents. In the mutilated checkerboard, you can think in terms of total area or in terms of pairing different-colored squares, and the color relationship exposes a constraint that area alone does not.

qa_facts.q: What is the Russian marriage problem, why is the answer no, and how does it match the mutilated checkerboard?
qa_facts.a: There are 32 bachelors and 32 unmarried women, and a matchmaker arranges 32 heterosexual marriages. Two bachelors die after a contest involving pierogies, leaving 62 survivors, 30 men and 32 women. The question is whether 31 heterosexual marriages can be formed. The answer is no, because each marriage needs one member of each group and the groups are unequal, so at most 30 marriages can form and two women are left without a partner. Dividing 62 people by two gives 31 pairs by total size, but that ignores which kinds of person each pair must contain, and no rearrangement creates another man. In the checkerboard, a domino covers two adjacent squares, one of each color, and removing two opposite corners removes two squares of the same color, so the colors are unequal even though 62 squares matches the area of 31 dominoes. Moving the dominoes around cannot change that imbalance.

qa_facts.q: What is analogical problem solving, and how does the Russian marriage problem serve as a source for the checkerboard?
qa_facts.a: Analogical problem solving uses the solution to a similar problem to guide the solution to a new one. The target problem is the one currently being solved, and a source problem shares relevant similarities with it. The Russian marriage problem is the source and the mutilated checkerboard is the target. Marriages correspond to dominoes, the two groups of people correspond to the two square colors, and a valid marriage needs one member of each group, just as a domino needs one square of each color. Removing two bachelors corresponds to removing two same-colored squares, since both leave an imbalance. Analogical transfer is the transfer from source to target, and the useful information is the relationship among the elements, not their identical appearance.

qa_facts.q: What is Duncker’s radiation problem, and how is it solved?
qa_facts.a: Duncker’s radiation problem describes a patient who has a malignant tumor in the stomach that cannot be operated on, and a ray can destroy the tumor only if high enough intensity reaches it at once. A high-intensity ray would also destroy the healthy tissue it passes through, and a low-intensity ray would spare the tissue but not destroy the tumor. The solution is several low-intensity rays converging on the tumor from different directions at the same time, so each path through the tissue gets low intensity while the combined intensity at the tumor is enough. Only about 10 percent of participants reach this without the helpful analogy.

qa_facts.q: How does the fortress problem correspond to Duncker’s radiation problem?
qa_facts.a: A rebel general has an army strong enough to take a dictator’s fortress, but mines on each road explode if a large force passes. Small groups can travel safely along different roads and arrive together, and combined they are strong enough to attack. The fortress corresponds to the tumor in Duncker’s radiation problem, the small groups to the low-intensity rays, and the roads to the paths through tissue. Sending the whole army down one road matches sending one high-intensity ray through healthy tissue. The groups have to arrive together, because merely dividing the army or lowering every ray’s intensity without combining the effects leaves the target requirement unmet.

qa_facts.q: What are noticing, mapping and applying in Gick and Holyoak’s analogy steps, and what happened when participants were reminded of the story?
qa_facts.a: Gick and Holyoak distinguished noticing that a source may be relevant to the target, mapping the correspondences between their elements and relationships, and applying the mapping to generate a parallel solution. Noticing is crucial and can be the hardest step. After reading the fortress story, only about 30 percent of participants solved the radiation problem, so having the story in memory did not guarantee they used it spontaneously. When they were told to think about the story they had read, success rose to about 75 percent. The reminder made the relevant source available for mapping and application. Surface features, such as a fortress, an army, a tumor or a ray, can hide a shared relationship, since a fortress and a tumor do not look alike, and making surface features more similar can make the relationship easier to notice.

qa_facts.q: What is the lightbulb problem, and how well does Duncker’s radiation problem work as a source for it?
qa_facts.a: Ruth finds an expensive laboratory lightbulb with a broken filament, and the surrounding glass is sealed, so she cannot open it. A brief, high-intensity laser would fuse the filament but also break the fragile glass, and a low-intensity beam would save the glass but not fuse the filament. The solution is several low-intensity lasers directed at the filament from different directions at once, so their combined effect fuses it while each part of the glass gets only a low-intensity beam. Duncker’s radiation problem acts as a source because the tumor and filament are targets needing a strong local effect, and healthy tissue and fragile glass are surroundings that a single strong approach would damage. The two also share surface features, since both direct a beam toward an internal target. About 81 percent of participants who knew the radiation problem solved the lightbulb problem, compared with about 10 percent in the control group.

qa_facts.q: What is the difference between surface features and structural features?
qa_facts.a: Surface features are the specific elements used to describe a problem, such as lightbulbs, lasers, tumors and rays, and similar objects can help a person notice that two situations may be related. Structural features are the underlying principle that governs the solution. In the radiation and fragile-glass problems, a strong ray or laser would damage the surroundings on its way to an internal target, so enough intensity must reach the target while the intensity along each path stays low, and that is why several low-intensity approaches must converge. Two lightbulb versions can keep the same surface features while changing the structure.

qa_facts.q: How did the fragile-glass and insufficient-intensity lightbulb sources compare as sources for the radiation problem?
qa_facts.a: In the fragile-glass version, a high-intensity beam would break the glass, which matches the healthy-tissue constraint, and about 69 percent of participants who read it solved the radiation problem. In the insufficient-intensity version, the laser can only make low-intensity beams that cannot fuse the filament, so beams are combined to get enough intensity, but there is no surrounding-damage constraint. About 33 percent of participants who read that one solved the radiation problem. Both sources use converging beams, but the different transfer rates go with the difference in underlying constraints.

qa_facts.q: What is analogical encoding?
qa_facts.a: Analogical encoding is comparing two problems and determining the similarities between them. Comparing source stories draws attention to relationships that appear in both, such as separate weak approaches combining at one target while constraints along the approaches prevent a single strong delivery. Having participants compare sources directs their reasoning toward the structural features, so a later target can be approached through the common relationship and does not depend entirely on the appearance of one familiar situation.

qa_facts.q: What is the analogical paradox, and what is the in vivo method?
qa_facts.a: The analogical paradox is the contrast between difficulty applying analogies in laboratory tasks and routine use of analogies in real-world settings. Scientists use about 3 to 15 analogies in a one-hour laboratory meeting. In vivo problem-solving research observes people solving problems in real-world settings, which keeps the ordinary context, but it can be time-consuming and researchers cannot isolate and control variables as in a more constrained experiment.

qa_facts.q: What is an expert, and what do experts do better and worse?
qa_facts.a: An expert is a person recognized as extremely knowledgeable or skilled in a field after devoting a large amount of time to learning, practicing and applying it. A chess expert can have spent roughly 10,000 to 20,000 hours studying and playing. Experts solve problems in their field faster and with a higher success rate than beginners, and they spend more time analyzing a problem before proceeding. But the advantage is specific to the field, and experts are no better than novices on problems outside it.

qa_facts.q: What did Chase and Simon (1973) find about chess recall?
qa_facts.a: Chase and Simon (1973) compared a chess master with a beginner who had fewer than 100 hours of chess experience. Each viewed a chessboard for five seconds and then tried to reproduce where the pieces were, using either actual game positions or random arrangements. The expert did much better for actual game positions, because long-term memory made meaningful arrangements available as chunks, groups of related information. For random arrangements those familiar chunks were not available, so the advantage reflects organized domain knowledge and not an equal advantage for every arrangement.

qa_facts.q: What did Chi et al. (1982) find when experts and novices sorted physics problems?
qa_facts.a: Chi et al. (1982) gave 24 physics problems to experts, who were physics professors, and novices, who were students with one semester of physics, and had them sort the problems into groups by similarity. Novices grouped by surface features, the appearance of the objects, so two problems with inclined planes were treated as alike. Experts grouped by structural features, the underlying principle. For example, the novice grouped problems 23 and 24 because both involve inclined planes, while the expert grouped problems 21 and 24 together through conservation of energy, even though 21 has a block and spring on a horizontal surface and 24 has blocks on an incline. The same problem 24 gets a different partner under the two organizations, and expertise changes which relationship is the basis for similarity, so knowledge becomes accessible through the principle that governs the solution.

qa_facts.q: What are the limits of expertise?
qa_facts.a: Experts spend more time analyzing a problem before proceeding, which can pay off in solving it efficiently, but the advantage is specific to the expert’s field. Expertise can make a person less open to new ways of looking at a problem, and too much knowledge can hinder creative problem solving when a familiar approach dominates. Flexible thinking sometimes means rejecting the usual procedure for a less frequently used one, since some problems require it.

qa_facts.q: What does creative problem solving involve beyond having an idea?
qa_facts.a: Creativity includes innovative thinking, novel ideas and new connections, and divergent thinking is open-ended and allows many potential solutions. Creative problem solving usually involves more than getting an idea, including a lengthy period of trial and error. Problem generation includes problem finding and fact finding, formulation includes defining the problem and finding ideas, solving includes evaluation and planning, and solution implementation means taking action. Ideas are necessary, since without them the process stops, but generating them does not evaluate, plan or carry out a response.
